prompt: How is the price of a spot instance set today?
hint: There has been no bidding since 2017.

choices.text: By an auction: the highest bids win the capacity and set the price
choices.why: That was roughly the model before 2017. Nobody bids now.

choices.text: As a fixed 90% off the on-demand price, the same for every type and zone
choices.why: Ninety percent is the most AWS describes, not a fixed rate; the real discount varies by pool and week.

choices.text: By the maximum price each customer sets on the request
choices.why: MaxPrice only adds a reason to be interrupted; it does not set what anybody pays.

choices.text: By AWS, per type and zone, from long-term supply and demand, moving gradually
choices.why: Right. The price of each pool changes over days, not minutes, and you pay it whatever maximum you set.

prompt: moto's spot price history shows 0.00001 USD an hour for m7i.large in every zone, dated 2006. How should that be read?
hint: Could any of it be a measurement?

choices.text: As the floor AWS keeps for spot, which a quiet zone can reach
choices.why: There is no such floor, and the date is three years before spot existed.

choices.text: As a real price from moto's catalogue, out of date by some years
choices.why: moto's catalogue of instance types is AWS's; its spot prices are not prices from anywhere.

choices.text: As a placeholder, because nothing moto reports about money is real
choices.why: Right. On AWS the same call returns real changes of price over the last 90 days, per zone.

choices.text: As what is left of the on-demand price once a 90% discount is applied
choices.why: A tenth of 0.16065 is 0.016065, not 0.00001; the number is not derived from anything.

prompt: Assume, for the arithmetic only, a spot discount of 70%. What do 5 spot m7i.large instances cost for 730 hours, at the on-demand price of 0.16065 USD an hour, in USD?
hint: You pay 30% of the on-demand price.

prompt: What does setting MaxPrice well below the on-demand price do to a spot instance?
hint: What do you pay, whatever the maximum?

choices.text: Lowers the bill to that maximum
choices.why: You pay the spot price of the pool, never your maximum.

choices.text: Moves the instance to a cheaper zone
choices.why: The maximum chooses nothing about placement.

choices.text: Protects it from interruptions while the price stays under the maximum
choices.why: AWS reclaims capacity whatever your maximum is; the maximum is an extra reason, never a shield.

choices.text: Adds a second reason to be interrupted, without lowering what you pay
choices.why: Right. If the pool's price rises above your maximum, the instance goes; the price you pay meanwhile is the same.

prompt: Match each spot option to what it means at an interruption.
hint: Three behaviours and the kind of request two of them need.

pairs.right: EBS volumes kept, started again when capacity returns
Memory written to the root volume first, resumed later
The request outlives the instance, which stop and hibernate need

right_distractors: A bid that keeps the instance against other customers

prompt: How much notice does AWS give before it takes a spot instance back?
hint: The interruption notice, not the recommendation.

choices.text: None: the instance stops without warning
choices.why: There is a notice, on the metadata path and in EventBridge.

choices.text: Two minutes
choices.why: Right. The notice appears two minutes before the instance is stopped, hibernated or terminated.

choices.text: Fifteen minutes, enough to finish most jobs
choices.why: Two minutes is all there is, which is why draining is a list of things to stop.

choices.text: Whatever the lifecycle hook's timeout says
choices.why: A hook can hold an instance the group is terminating; it does not lengthen a spot interruption.

prompt: On AWS, until an interruption is scheduled, the metadata path spot/instance-action answers with the HTTP status ___.
hint: Not found.

prompt: spot-watch.sh, pointed at moto, printed no notice (500). Why is treating every answer but 200 as "not yet" the right design?
hint: What would a listener that exits on surprises miss?

choices.text: Stopping on a surprise would end the listening, and miss the notice when it came
choices.why: Right. The only answer that should change its behaviour is a notice; everything else is a reason to look again in five seconds.

choices.text: Because AWS answers 500 while there is no notice yet, exactly as moto did here
choices.why: AWS answers 404; the 500 was moto not implementing the path.

choices.text: Because a 500 means the interruption was cancelled
choices.why: Nothing cancels a notice; and no 500 is part of the documented behaviour.

choices.text: So that it can be tested against moto at all
choices.why: That is a convenience it happens to give, not the reason the design is right on AWS.

prompt: A queue worker on spot gets its interruption notice. Put the drain in order.
hint: Stop first, finish second, hand back third.
items: Stop reading new messages from the queue
Finish the message in hand, or checkpoint it
Leave unfinished messages undeleted, so they become visible again
AWS terminates the instance at the time in the notice
trap: Reading one more message after the notice starts work the two minutes cannot finish.

prompt: An instance receives a rebalance recommendation. What can it count on?
hint: It is a hint, not a promise.

choices.text: An interruption notice within the next two minutes
choices.why: The two may arrive together, far apart, or the notice may never come.

choices.text: That AWS will not interrupt it before it has been replaced
choices.why: Nothing guarantees that; the notice can come at any moment after, or before, the recommendation.

choices.text: Elevated risk, nothing more: it runs on for hours or days
choices.why: Right. That is why a group uses it to launch a replacement early, and nothing waits on it.

choices.text: Fifteen minutes before the notice, as a fixed lead
choices.why: There is no fixed lead; the timing varies, and sometimes there is no recommendation at all.

prompt: A mixed group has OnDemandBaseCapacity 3 and OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity 20. At a desired capacity of 13, how many of its instances are spot?
hint: Take the base off first, then split the rest.

prompt: Why does the lesson's group allow four instance types rather than one?
hint: AWS interrupts by pool.

choices.text: Each type in each zone is its own pool of spare capacity, and more pools mean fewer moments with nowhere to launch
choices.why: Right. Four types over three zones is twelve pools; one type is three, and they can run dry together.

choices.text: So that the group can pick a faster type when the load rises
choices.why: The types are chosen to be interchangeable; nothing picks by speed.

choices.text: Because a mixed instances policy refuses fewer than four
choices.why: One override is accepted; four is a choice about pools.

choices.text: To spread the on-demand base over four prices
choices.why: The base is about which instances cannot be interrupted, not about prices.

prompt: moto launched the lesson's mixed group as ten m7i.large, all on demand. What would AWS have launched?
hint: Base two, then a quarter of eight.

choices.text: Ten on-demand instances too, until a scaling policy asked for spot
choices.why: The distribution applies from the first launch; no policy is needed.

choices.text: Two on demand and eight spot
choices.why: That leaves out the 25% of the eight above the base, which are on demand too.

choices.text: Four on demand and six spot, spread over the types and zones
choices.why: Right. Two from the base, two from 25% of the other eight, and six spot instances chosen by the allocation strategy.

choices.text: Ten spot instances, with two kept as a base in reserve
choices.why: The base is two running on-demand instances, not a reserve of spot ones.

prompt: Somebody adds m7g.large to the overrides of the lesson's group and changes nothing else. What goes wrong on AWS?
hint: What does the g mean, and what image is in the template?

choices.text: Nothing: overrides change only the instance type, and the image adapts to whichever processor it lands on
choices.why: An image is built for one architecture; it does not adapt.

choices.text: m7g.large has less memory, so the group rejects the override
choices.why: It has the same 2 vCPUs and 8 GiB as the others; size is not the problem.

choices.text: Arm types are not offered as spot
choices.why: They are; the problem is the image, not the market.

choices.text: The x86_64 image cannot boot on Arm; m7g.large needs an override with an arm64 image
choices.why: Right. A mixed group can carry Arm and x86 together, but each architecture needs an image of its own.

prompt: Which of these are true of the spot allocation strategies? Choose all that apply.
hint: Risk first, price first, or both.

choices.text: price-capacity-optimized picks the least-risk pools and the cheapest of those
choices.why: And it is AWS's recommendation for most workloads.

choices.text: capacity-optimized picks by risk of interruption, whatever the price
choices.why: It ignores price inside the pools it trusts.

choices.text: lowest-price is the safest, because cheap pools are the quiet ones
choices.why: Cheap pools are often the ones most likely to be taken back.

choices.text: The strategy also decides how many instances are on demand
choices.why: That is the base and the percentage; the strategy only chooses pools for spot.

choices.text: moto 5.2.3 stored the strategy and launched no spot instance
choices.why: The description kept it, and every instance came out on demand.

prompt: Which of these are good candidates for spot? Choose all that apply.
hint: Can any one instance vanish and the work carry on?

choices.text: Workers reading from a queue
choices.why: An unfinished message comes back after its visibility timeout.

choices.text: The only PostgreSQL server of the shop
choices.why: One instance holding state is exactly what an interruption destroys.

choices.text: CI build agents
choices.why: An interrupted build is run again, and builds are made to be repeatable.

choices.text: Stateless API instances above an on-demand base
choices.why: Requests are short and the base keeps the service up through an interruption.

choices.text: A six-hour report job that cannot checkpoint
choices.why: The longer the job, the likelier an interruption lands inside it and starts it again.

prompt: An application needs 20 minutes to warm its caches before it serves well, and its spot instances are interrupted about once an hour. What is the verdict?
hint: Compare the start-up with the life between interruptions.

choices.text: Good fit: the discount pays for the warm-up
choices.why: A third of every instance's life is spent warming; the discount buys capacity that is not serving.

choices.text: A poor fit unless the warm-up is made shorter, because a third of each instance's hour goes on starting
choices.why: Right. Spot suits work whose start-up is short against the time between interruptions.

choices.text: Fine, as long as the lifecycle hook gives it longer to drain
choices.why: Draining is not the problem; starting is, and a hook does not lengthen a spot interruption anyway.

choices.text: Good fit if the group uses capacity-optimized
choices.why: A strategy can lower the interruption rate; it cannot make a twenty-minute warm-up free.

prompt: A service needs three instances to answer at all, and normally runs ten. How should a mixed group set its base?
hint: The base is the part an interruption cannot take.

choices.text: OnDemandBaseCapacity of at least 3
choices.why: Right. The minimum the service needs is on demand, and the rest can be discounted.

choices.text: A base of 0 and an on-demand percentage of 30, which also gives three
choices.why: Three of ten only while the group is at ten; at a lower count the percentage gives fewer.

choices.text: A base of 10, so nothing is ever at risk
choices.why: Then the group has no spot at all and the discount is gone.

choices.text: No base, with capacity rebalancing to cover the gap
choices.why: Rebalancing replaces at-risk instances when it can; it does not keep a floor that cannot be taken.

prompt: Which question decides whether something belongs on spot?
hint: Not how important it is.

choices.text: Whether it is production or test
choices.why: A production API can run mostly on spot and a test database must not.

choices.text: Whether its instance type has a large discount this week
choices.why: A large discount on something that cannot be interrupted is a gamble that loses eventually.

choices.text: How many instances it runs
choices.why: A group of fifty holding state is as unsafe as one.

choices.text: What one interruption would cost
choices.why: Right. If any instance can vanish and the work carries on, spot is a discount.

prompt: A group has --capacity-rebalance. One of its spot instances receives a rebalance recommendation. What does the group do on AWS?
hint: Launch first.

choices.text: Terminates it at once, then launches a replacement
choices.why: That order would leave a gap; rebalancing launches first.

choices.text: Launches a replacement in a pool at lower risk, then terminates the instance at risk
choices.why: Right. Capacity stays up, and the lifecycle hook, if any, still gets its turn on the leaving instance.

choices.text: Waits for the interruption notice, then replaces it
choices.why: The point of the setting is to act before the notice, while there is time.

choices.text: Moves it to on demand
choices.why: An instance cannot change market; a new one is launched instead.

prompt: Half a group runs on spot at a 50% discount, the rest on demand, all of one type. By what percentage is the group's bill lower than all on demand?
hint: The discount times the share on spot.

prompt: moto's lifecycle hook came back with a queue in us-east-1 and a role in account 1234567890, though neither was given. What would AWS show?
hint: What was in the call?

choices.text: No notification target and no role
choices.why: Right. Without a target, the instance's own drain script completes the action when it is done.

choices.text: The same two ARNs, which AWS fills in as defaults
choices.why: AWS invents no target; those ARNs are moto's filler.

choices.text: An error, because a hook needs a notification target
choices.why: A hook without one is valid; it is completed with complete-lifecycle-action.

choices.text: A queue and a role created for the hook in the group's own account
choices.why: AWS creates neither on your behalf for a hook.

prompt: A group's termination hook has a 120-second timeout and default CONTINUE. A spot interruption notice arrives for one of its instances. How long does the instance have?
hint: Whose clock is it?

choices.text: Two minutes plus the hook's 120 seconds
choices.why: The hook does not add to AWS's reclaim; AWS takes the capacity at the time in the notice.

choices.text: As long as it takes, since CONTINUE waits for the script
choices.why: CONTINUE is what happens when the timeout passes; nothing waits forever.

choices.text: Two minutes, whatever the hook says
choices.why: Right. A hook holds an instance the group is terminating; it cannot hold back capacity AWS is reclaiming.

choices.text: 120 seconds counted from when the hook is completed
choices.why: The hook's clock is irrelevant to a reclaim, and two minutes is AWS's.

prompt: Why does the spot-watch.sh script poll every five seconds rather than every minute?
hint: What is the whole budget?

choices.text: Because the metadata service refuses a token older than a minute
choices.why: The token asks for 300 seconds; the interval is not about the token.

choices.text: Because the notice only stays on the path for five seconds
choices.why: It stays until the instance goes.

choices.text: A minute's delay would spend half of the two minutes before draining began
choices.why: Right. Five seconds leaves almost the whole notice for stopping work.

choices.text: Because AWS bills metadata calls by the minute, so polling faster costs nothing more
choices.why: Metadata calls are not billed.
